rounds.text: Jindal Supreme (India) Ltd trades at a modest P/E of 22.6 [E1], yet the underlying business exhibits elite profitability metrics with an ROE of 26.28% and an ROCE of 19.69% [E8, E9]. This superior financial performance is supported by robust multi-year compounding, featuring a 5-year sales growth of 26% and an explosive 542% profit growth over the trailing twelve months [E13, E18]. Operating margins are steadily expanding, climbing by 4 percentage points to 6% over the last three years in a non-cyclical earnings profile [E22, E23, E37]. Valuation models underscore significant upside, with a DCF intrinsic value pointing to a substantial margin of safety of 45.8%, while the reverse DCF indicates the market price only prices in a modest 9.6% earnings growth against an 18.0% base case [E33, E34, E35]. Conceded: operating cash flow is negative at Rs -6 Cr with a cash conversion of -0.26x, and debt exceeds net worth at a leverage of 1.27x [E25, E26, E29].

Conceded: [E18] shows strong profit growth in the trailing twelve months, but the reported profits are starkly disconnected from actual liquidity generation. Operating cash flow for March 2026 has plunged into negative territory at Rs -6 Cr, producing an alarming cash conversion ratio of -0.26x [E25, E26]. Free cash flow is similarly distressed at Rs -15 Cr [E27], meaning operating cash flow represents a negligible 2% of operating profit [E28]. Furthermore, the financial statements explicitly flag a critical risk that the company might be capitalizing its interest costs [E39], casting serious doubt on the quality of those headline earnings. This aggressive cash burn is compounded by rising financial leverage, with borrowings climbing from Rs 99 Cr to Rs 123 Cr, pushing the debt-to-equity ratio above parity to 1.27x [E29, E30]. Finally, shareholders receive zero return in cash, as the dividend yield sits squarely at 0.00% [E3].

Conceded: [E25, E26, E27] show negative operating and free cash flow alongside a low cash conversion ratio in March 2026. However, the bear's alarm over headline earnings is neutralized by stellar profitability metrics, including a trailing twelve-month profit growth of 542% and a 5-year CAGR of 35% [E16, E18, E38]. Furthermore, the business generates exceptional returns on capital, featuring a 26.2% ROE and a 19.7% ROCE that drastically outperform sector benchmarks [E8, E9, E12]. While borrowings climbed to Rs 123 Cr [E30], this leverage supports a non-cyclical operation demonstrating expanding operational efficiency, with operating margins rising 4 percentage points to 6% over three years alongside a four-year increasing trend [E22, E23, E37]. Finally, the intrinsic valuation offers a robust 45.8% margin of safety, and the reverse DCF indicates the market price only prices in a modest 9.6% growth rate compared to the 18.0% base case [E33, E34, E35].

Conceded: [E16, E18, E38] show strong reported profit growth, but these figures are fundamentally undermined by the company's inability to convert that profit into actual cash [E25, E28]. While the bull highlights high ROE and ROCE [E8, E9, E12], these metrics are rendered questionable by the fact that operating cash flow was negative Rs 6 Cr and free cash flow was negative Rs 15 Cr in March 2026 [E26, E27]. The bull’s reliance on expanding margins [E22, E23] ignores the reality that the company is simultaneously increasing its debt burden to Rs 123 Cr, resulting in a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.27x that signals significant leverage risk [E29, E30]. Furthermore, the suggestion that the business is non-cyclical [E37] does not mitigate the specific warning that the company might be capitalizing interest costs, which artificially inflates reported profitability at the expense of cash quality [E39]. Finally, the bull’s reliance on a 45.8% margin of safety [E34] is speculative when the company pays a 0.00% dividend yield, meaning shareholders receive no tangible return while the firm burns cash [E3].
